title: IAM, Resource Hierarchy, and Separation of Duties
bodyMarkdown:
## Why the resource hierarchy is your first security control

Google Cloud arranges resources as **Organization → Folders → Projects → Resources**. IAM policies and **Organization Policies** set on a higher node are **inherited** downward. This makes the hierarchy the backbone of governance: design it well and most guardrails fall into place; design it badly and you fight per-project drift forever.

- **Organization node:** the root. Holds org-wide IAM and the org-policy baseline.
- **Folders:** group projects by department, team, or environment (prod/non-prod). Bind IAM and policies here for inheritance.
- **Projects:** the unit of billing, quota, and isolation (blast radius).

### Design guidance

- Group by **department or environment** with folders; avoid one giant project.
- Apply a **secure baseline** of org policies at the top and relax only with justification.
- Keep prod and non-prod in **separate folders/projects** so policies and access differ.

## IAM model

An IAM **policy** binds **members** (users, groups, service accounts, federated identities) to **roles** on a **resource**.

| Role type | Use it for |
|---|---|
| **Predefined** | Day-to-day; curated, least-privilege per service (e.g., `roles/storage.objectViewer`). |
| **Custom** | When predefined roles are too broad and you need an exact permission set. |
| **Basic** (Owner/Editor/Viewer) | Avoid in production — far too broad. |

### Best practices

- **Bind roles to Google Groups**, not individual emails — easier to audit and offboard.
- Grant at the **lowest node** that satisfies the need (least privilege).
- Use **IAM Conditions** to scope by time, resource name, or request attributes.
- Prefer **service account impersonation** and **Workload Identity Federation** over long-lived keys.

## Separation of duties (SoD)

No single person should hold conflicting powers (e.g., **deploy** code **and** **approve** its release). Model SoD by splitting permissions across **distinct, non-overlapping groups**:

- `deployers` group → deploy permissions.
- `approvers` group → release/attestor permissions (pairs well with Binary Authorization attestors).
- A separate `org-policy-admins` group holds `roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin`, so workload owners cannot weaken guardrails.

SoD is **preventive**; after-the-fact auditing is only **detective**. Combine both, but do not rely on auditing alone.

## Putting it together

A typical secure layout:

- Org policies (deny external IP, restrict locations, disable default network) at the **org node**.
- Folder-level IAM for each department; project-level only for fine exceptions.
- Groups for every functional role; impersonation/JIT for elevated access.
- Aggregated audit-log sink at the org for accountability.
